video_title: Can public EV chargers be as reliable as gas stations?
gist: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna (the DC fast-charging joint venture owned by eight automakers including BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis and Toyota), lays out the operating and capital plan behind a 30,000-bay-by-2030 target: 143 sites and ~1,300 bays live across 30+ states today, just under 600 sites contracted with 400 stuck in permitting, flat 39c/kWh pricing on 400kW chargers, and a deliberate refusal to chase NEVI grants, on-site batteries, or amenity monetization. He argues the US EV sales downturn, the expiring consumer credit and clawed-back DOE charger grants are irrelevant to a network being built for 2028+ demand, and that permitting and utility power access — not capital or EV adoption — are the binding constraints.

themes.theme: Four-phase map of US public charging

insights.claim: US public DC fast charging has moved through four distinct phases — 2010-era 'put chargers in the ground anywhere' single nodes, 2017-era network buildout (Tesla, EVgo in cities, Electrify America as the Tesla answer), a post-COVID reliability-and-uptime phase, and a current fourth phase competing on experience beyond reliability.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Tells investors which capability set now differentiates charging operators — uptime is table stakes, so screen networks on site amenity, canopy and land strategy rather than on charger count.

insights.claim: Reliability is now table stakes rather than a differentiator in EV charging, analogous to how diners do not research which restaurants cause food poisoning but instead judge menu, price and ambiance.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Charging networks that market only uptime are competing on a commoditized attribute; pricing power will shift to whoever owns the site experience.
insights.quote: folks typically don't look to see which restaurants will cause food poisoning. They it's kind of taken as a uh kind of like the table stakes

insights.claim: The 2020-2022 reliability crisis was caused by utilization rising against infrastructure built for low usage — a six-bay site effectively becoming a two-bay site under queuing exposed operators that lacked spare-parts supply chains or field service processes.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Uptime failure is an operations/supply-chain problem, not a hardware problem — due diligence on charging operators should focus on parts inventory and labor networks.

insights.claim: The binding EV adoption constraint is charging anxiety rather than range anxiety — the question of whether a charger will work on arrival, not how far the car can go.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Reframes the EV adoption bottleneck away from battery specs and toward charging infrastructure quality, favoring infrastructure over battery-range plays.
insights.quote: the biggest issue today in the or even back then was infrastructure reliability charging anxiety not range anxiety

insights.claim: Direct driver research at deployed sites, not pre-deployment interviews, is what surfaces real requirements — roughly 1,000 responses from customer clinics run at live sites in June identified affordability, night lighting/safety, canopy coverage, car-care items like trash cans and squeegees, and amenities as the demands beyond reliability.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Concrete list of features that will define the next competitive round in charging capex — canopies and lighting become table-stakes cost items, not optional.

insights.claim: Ayanna had turned on site number 143 as of mid-August 2026, roughly 1,300 charging bays live across just over 30 states, with 150 sites expected within a week — against a stated target of 30,000 charging bays by 2030.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Implies a required ~23x expansion in under four years; a hard benchmark to track whether the OEM charging JV is credible or will miss badly.

insights.claim: Ayanna has just under 600 sites contracted across the US, of which only about 200 are in construction or live, leaving roughly 400 sites stuck in the permitting pipeline.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Two-thirds of the contracted pipeline is gated by permitting, so permitting-reform outcomes are the single largest swing factor on the buildout curve.

insights.claim: Ayanna's unit economics scale off a standard site of roughly 10 bays, where each charger serves two bays, so the 30,000-bay goal implies on the order of 3,000 sites and 1,500 chargers per thousand bays.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Lets analysts convert the headline bay target into charger-hardware order volumes and site-acquisition requirements.

insights.claim: Ayanna went from one employee in February 2024 to just under 100 people in Raleigh-Durham, North Carolina, building the business from zero rather than as a division of an existing company.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: A ~100-person team supporting a 3,000-site target implies heavy reliance on third-party labor and a large G&A scaling risk.

insights.claim: Over 70% of Ayanna's build will be attached to an amenity — either 'rechargery at' sites co-located with marquee partners like Wawa, Sheetz, Casey's and other convenience-store operators, or full ground-up rechargeries where Ayanna builds the amenity itself; only about half a dozen full ground-up rechargeries are open today with dozens in permitting.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: The freestanding gas-station-replacement vision is still a small minority of deployed assets; convenience-store chains are the near-term distribution channel and beneficiaries.

insights.claim: 70% of Ayanna's investment goes to sites inside cities rather than remote highway corridors, but deliberately placed adjacent to interstates so a single site serves both metro residents and pass-through travelers.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: The 'stacked use case' urban-edge siting strategy is how the company intends to beat the industry's ~15% utilization problem — watch it as the key operating metric.

insights.claim: Ayanna targets four distinct customer segments at the same site — long-distance vacation travelers, daily commuters who occasionally miss a home charge, apartment dwellers and older-home residents with no L2 access, and fleets including Uber and rideshare drivers plus service businesses.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Stacking four demand curves on one asset is the mechanism for raising utilization above breakeven; single-segment charging operators are structurally disadvantaged.

insights.claim: Ayanna already has continuous coast-to-coast coverage on I-70 from California to Raleigh and I-95 coverage from New York City to Florida, with I-5 from Seattle toward Los Angeles currently being filled in.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Corridor completion is the precondition for the network effect the company is betting on; I-5 completion is the next observable milestone.

themes.theme: Charging unit economics and demand charges

insights.claim: A DC fast charging port generally needs 15-25% utilization to cover costs and loses money below 10-15%, while industry-wide utilization hovers around 15% — putting the average charging asset at or below breakeven.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host
insights.so_what: Sets the hurdle rate for any charging investment: sites must clear ~20% utilization or the economics do not work without subsidy or ancillary revenue.

insights.claim: Ayanna prices at a flat 39 cents per kilowatt hour while deploying 400kW chargers, deliberately running the highest-power hardware at below-industry-average prices.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host
insights.so_what: A concrete price benchmark to measure competitors against; the combination of high power and low price compresses margin and raises demand-charge exposure simultaneously.

insights.claim: Ayanna deliberately chose not to install on-site batteries despite having the opportunity early on, on the reasoning that batteries improve Ayanna's financials but do not improve the driver experience and would distract from site buildout speed.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Bearish near-term signal for stationary-storage vendors selling demand-charge mitigation into charging — the largest OEM-backed network is explicitly deferring that capex to 'future years'.
insights.quote: we had opportunities to put batteries in place early on and we made conscious decisions not to go do that because it's very easy to get distracted

insights.claim: Cost control on G&A, not electricity price, is the lever that determines charging affordability — high marketing, development and overhead costs force operators to raise the price at the bay.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Implies charging network margins are an opex-discipline story; screen operators on overhead per bay rather than on hardware specs.

insights.claim: Ayanna does not yet know whether amenity and retail sales will be a meaningful revenue line and is explicitly refusing to build teams to monetize dwell time, despite drivers sitting for 20 minutes versus 5 at a gas pump.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: The gas-station analogy (money made on snacks, not fuel) is not yet the business model here — retail-attach upside is unproven optionality, not underwritten revenue.
insights.quote: We're in the business of selling electrons. That's what the business is.

insights.claim: Ayanna must become profitable on a standalone basis and is not a loss leader for the OEM owners, because if charging infrastructure itself is not profitable, electrification as a whole will not work.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Rules out the assumption that OEMs will indefinitely subsidize the network — the JV carries genuine standalone financial risk if utilization stalls.
insights.quote: Ayanna is financially independent or financially independent. It's a separate entity, right? And so we have to be profitable over time.

insights.claim: Charging profitability requires a higher density of vehicles sold than the US currently has, meaning the industry's economics are gated on EV penetration reaching levels already seen in other markets.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Charging network returns are a leveraged bet on US EV sales penetration, not a defensive infrastructure holding.

themes.theme: Permitting, power access and utility relations

insights.claim: Construction is not the bottleneck in charging infrastructure — Ayanna built and energized a site in Tucumcari, New Mexico in six days, while permits and utility power access are the actual constraints.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Deployment forecasts should be modeled off permitting and interconnection queues, not construction capacity; jurisdictional permitting speed is the alpha variable.
insights.quote: We built the site in 6 days.

insights.claim: Ayanna always installs its own meter and transformer from the utility regardless of whether the site is co-located at an existing convenience store or built greenfield, so partnering with a Wawa or Sheetz does not shortcut interconnection.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Kills the assumption that host-site partnerships reduce utility lead time — interconnection demand from charging is fully incremental for utilities and transformer suppliers.

insights.claim: Ayanna manages the permitting bottleneck by maintaining a deliberately oversized site funnel, treating fast-permitting jurisdictions like Kansas as 'short cycle' sites to build network coverage while multi-year sites fill in later.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: A reusable model for any distributed-infrastructure developer facing permitting variance: build pipeline width, then sequence by cycle time rather than by market attractiveness.

insights.claim: Utilities never refuse EV charging on principle but do gate sites on feeder capacity — Ayanna has walked away from sites quoted at 3 to 5 year power timelines, and is holding a California site where it bought the land before discovering insufficient power, deferring the build to 2028.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Distribution feeder capacity, not utility willingness, is what kills charging sites — a direct read-through to grid-upgrade and transformer demand.

insights.claim: Ayanna is using utility flexibility programs rather than hardware to manage grid constraints, including PG&E's flex connect program for peak-hour demand mitigation and deliberately undersized transformers paired with whole-site energy management.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Flexible interconnection is substituting for storage capex at charging sites — a demand driver for site energy-management software over batteries.

insights.claim: Ayanna's relationship with utilities is structurally symbiotic rather than adversarial because utilities sell electricity to businesses and Ayanna buys from them to resell to consumers, despite utilities profiting from demand charges and some running competing networks in states like Florida.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Downplays a real conflict of interest the host raised; watch whether utility-owned networks in Florida become a competitive constraint on Ayanna's largest state footprint.

themes.theme: Reliability operating model and site design

insights.claim: Reliability rests on three ingredients — in-house alerting/monitoring/diagnostics tooling, operational response processes with parts stocked in hubs near sites and labor nearby, and a 'driver first' culture creating bias toward action.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for assessing whether a charging network can actually deliver uptime, applicable to diligence on any distributed-asset service business.

insights.claim: Ayanna rolls a truck with a Pelican case of parts to any site within 24 hours of a single customer-reported charging problem, running a 'health check' to validate the issue rather than dismissing it as driver error.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: A quantified service-level standard that is expensive at scale — a direct cost item to watch as site count grows 20x.

insights.claim: Ayanna refuses to publish uptime or utilization statistics externally, keeping reliability metrics internal while competitors such as Tesla publicly boast 99% uptime.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Absence of disclosed uptime data is itself a diligence flag; investors cannot yet verify the core reliability claim of the OEM network.

insights.claim: Gas station pump reliability is materially lower than consumers assume — there is public data on gas station performance that would surprise people, as evidenced by yellow bags over broken handles.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'as reliable as a gas station' bar as lower than assumed, meaning the real EV differentiator is mean-time-to-repair, not zero failures.

insights.claim: Ayanna's sites are deliberately non-uniform, built by converting distressed real estate — a 100-year-old shuttered gas station in Apex, North Carolina, an old car dealership, and a former Subway restaurant have all been converted into rechargeries.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Adaptive reuse of dead auto-retail and fuel real estate is a lower-cost path to urban charging sites — a signal for owners of obsolete gas station and dealership parcels.

insights.claim: Zoning constraints are being routed around creatively — the Apex, North Carolina site is legally classified as a bakery with a local entrepreneur selling baked goods, because zoning prohibited a refueling center but permitted a restaurant or bakery.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Shows local zoning codes have not caught up to EV charging as a land use — a recurring friction and a source of regulatory arbitrage for nimble developers.
insights.quote: Oh, so it's it's technically a bakery with chargers. Exactly.

insights.claim: Ayanna staffs its amenity sites with zero permanent human employees, controlling access through QR codes that in some cases require an active charging session, plus security cameras, lighting, and occasional contracted local security patrols.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: The amenity model is unmanned by design, which is how it stays cheaper than a staffed convenience store — but it also caps retail attach revenue.

insights.claim: Only about 30% of Ayanna's deployed sites currently have canopies, despite canopy coverage being one of the top driver requests, because site constraints prevent it everywhere.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: A measurable gap between the marketed 'gas station experience' and what is actually built; track canopy penetration as a proxy for capex intensity per site.

themes.theme: US EV downturn, policy exposure and OEM commitment

insights.claim: Ayanna is explicitly not building a grant-funded network — it pursued NEVI money for only one or two sites and never collected or spent it, and is not actively seeking federal or state grants.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Insulates the largest OEM charging JV from the Trump administration's NEVI clawbacks — a differentiator versus operators whose pipelines depended on DOE corridor grants.
insights.quote: we are not looking to build out a NEVI funded network. We're not we're not actively going out there and trying to go find grants.

insights.claim: The US EV market backdrop is deteriorating on multiple fronts simultaneously — the consumer EV credit ends this month, the charger construction credit goes away next year, and NEVI grants have been clawed back or eliminated by the Trump administration, while US EV sales slow even as markets elsewhere boom.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host
insights.so_what: Defines the exact policy cliff dates US EV and charging exposures must survive; contrast with non-US markets argues for geographic rotation in EV supply chain positioning.

insights.claim: Ayanna's CEO is unworried about launching into the US EV downturn because EVs win on product attributes — acceleration, quiet operation, falling battery prices, rising charge speeds and range — and better products historically displace incumbents regardless of near-term policy.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: The bull case rests entirely on product substitution rather than subsidy, which is either genuine conviction or the only argument available to a subsidy-independent operator.

insights.claim: Automakers cancelling EV models and pulling back on EV sales are still expected to stay committed to charging infrastructure investment, because the debate is only over whether the electric share reaches 20%, 30% or 50% — not whether the future is electric.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Watch for any of the eight OEM shareholders reducing their Ayanna commitment — that would be the real signal of capitulation on US electrification, ahead of model cancellations.

insights.claim: The US charging market is at roughly the second inning by the CEO's own analogy, with vehicle sales not going to zero and each new model cohort offering longer range and faster charging that will lift adoption.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Frames current weak utilization as an early-cycle artifact rather than a structural ceiling — the crux of the entire charging investment case.
insights.quote: if this was a baseball game, we're probably still in the second inning, honestly

themes.theme: Network effects, capital access and the Ionity comparison

insights.claim: Ionity, the equivalent European automaker charging joint venture, has matured to the point where it no longer needs OEM funding and can attract infrastructure funds and bank financing, operating in a market where EV sales grow 30%+ versus shrinking US sales.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host
insights.so_what: Provides the template and timeline for when charging assets become institutionally financeable — and shows US operators are years behind because of sales-growth divergence.

insights.claim: Ayanna claims to be well capitalized for its current goals and is not pursuing outside capital, declining to give a timeline for reaching Ionity-style access to infrastructure funds and bank debt.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: No visible path yet to cheaper third-party capital means the 30,000-bay target remains dependent on the eight OEMs' balance sheets during an EV downturn.

insights.claim: Charging follows a telecom-style network effect where individual site performance is secondary — a single site on a corridor underperforms, but utilization across all sites rises once the corridor is complete, the same way a cell phone usable in only one town is worthless.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Justifies cross-subsidizing weak sites from strong ones and means site-level utilization data is a misleading way to value a charging network mid-buildout.

insights.claim: Ayanna's execution is sequenced as annual gates in a multi-wave strategy — 2024 prove you can build differentiated sites, 2025 prove national network coverage, 2026 build scale and density in key geographic markets.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit yardstick — if 2026 does not deliver visible metro density, the strategy is behind schedule.

insights.claim: A site in Gary, Indiana that is only three or four days old is already outpacing utilization at California sites open six to nine months, and Ayanna now runs about 20 sites in Florida making it one of the largest high-power networks in that state.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Contradicts the consensus that charging capital should follow EV density to California — underserved secondary markets may offer better utilization per dollar because supply, not demand, is scarce there.
insights.quote: we just opened the site in Gary Gary, Indiana. Um it's three days old or 4 days old and it's doing really well.

themes.theme: Driver experience, plug-and-charge and competition with Tesla

insights.claim: Ayanna has deliberately built no mobile app and has no intention of building one, instead supporting 14 different third-party apps plus credit card readers on every station, on the reasoning that every OEM plus ChargePoint and Presto already have apps.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Rejects the consumer-app land grab that charging networks have chased for a decade — bearish for the strategic value of charging-network consumer apps as an asset.
insights.quote: the one thing you don't do is download an INA app because there is no ion app.

insights.claim: Plug-and-charge and auto-charge are active for most of Ayanna's eight OEM investors with the rest launching this year, and have also been enabled for Ford, Rivian and Volvo drivers who are not shareholders.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Non-shareholder OEM enablement shows Ayanna optimizing for volume over exclusivity — the network is being positioned as neutral infrastructure, not an OEM walled garden.

insights.claim: Plug-and-charge will become the default charging authentication method within a few years, eliminating card fumbling entirely.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Payment-terminal and RFID hardware in charging is a declining attach; the value migrates to vehicle-network identity and settlement software.

insights.claim: Ayanna's stated value proposition against Tesla — which holds roughly half the ports in the country and boasts 99% uptime — is delivering an integrated end-to-end experience including navigation, routing and search optimization for eight OEM brands rather than one manufacturer.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: The competitive moat is in-vehicle software integration across eight brands, not hardware — watch OEM navigation integrations as the real scoreboard versus Tesla.

insights.claim: Ayanna is moving from OEM charging discounts to a dealership sales channel, placing charging packages and discounted electricity pricing into the EV purchase decision as a competitive selling point at point of sale.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Bundled charging packages become a new EV price-competition vector; OEMs without a network partner lose a lever as the consumer tax credit disappears.

insights.claim: The CEO's stated top risk is not power access, competition or capex returns but organizational maturity — scaling from a startup to a 100-person, 150-site operator fast enough without compromising the driver experience, having compressed what feels like five to seven normal startup years into two and a half.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: Management identifies execution scaling, not market or policy risk, as the binding constraint — the classic failure mode for infrastructure rollouts at exactly this size.

insights.claim: The CEO defines success as the moment people stop talking about charging reliability altogether, analogous to Verizon's 'can you hear me now' era ending, and hopes that inflection arrives as soon as next year.
insights.speaker: Seth Cutler, CEO of Ayanna
insights.so_what: An aggressive near-term timeline the CEO put on record — a checkable claim about when charging ceases to be a purchase objection for US EV buyers.
insights.quote: I'm honestly hoping it's it's next year.
